editorial_contributions.text:
Consider a bounded subset \(S\) of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) and recall that the diameter of \(S\) is the supremum of the Euclidean distance between two points of \(S\). The Borsuk number \(a(S)\) of \(S\) is the smallest number of subsets that \(S\) can be partitioned into such that each of these subsets has diameter less than the diameter of \(S\). \textit{K. Borsuk}'s conjecture [Fundam. Math. 20, 177--190 (1933; JFM 59.0560.01)] states that \(a(S)\) is always at most \(d+1\) but this conjecture is now known to be false [\textit{J. Kahn} and \textit{G. Kalai}, Bull. Am. Math. Soc., New Ser. 29, No. 1, 60--62 (1993; Zbl 0786.52002)].

This article gives characterizations of the finite subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with Borsuk number \(4\) in terms of the extremizers for the Vázsonyi problem and of the vertices of Reuleaux polyhedra.

The extremizers for the Vázsonyi problem are the unit diameter subsets of \(n\) points of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) containing \(2n-2\) pairs of points at unit distance, which is the largest possible number of such pairs as conjectured by E. Vázsonyi (see [\textit{P. Erdős}, Am. Math. Mon. 53, 248--250 (1946; Zbl 0060.34805)]) and proved independently by \textit{B. Grünbaum} [Bull. Res. Council Israel, Sect. A 6, 77--78 (1956; Zbl 0074.36304)], \textit{A. Heppes} [Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hung. 7, 465--466 (1956; Zbl 0073.39102)], and \textit{S. Straszewicz} [Bull. Acad. Pol. Sci., Cl. III 5, 39--40 (1957; Zbl 0077.14204)].

Reuleaux polyhedra form a subclass of ball polyhedra: consider a finite, unit diameter subset \(V\) of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) whose circumradius is less than \(1\). The ball polyhedron of \(V\) is the convex body \(\mathcal{B}(V)\) obtained by intersecting the unit Euclidean balls centered at the points from \(V\). The boundary of a ball polyhedron can be decomposed in a natural way into vertices, circular arcs, and spherical polygons and one can consider the graph \(G(V)\) formed by these vertices and circular arcs. When \(G(V)\) admits \(V\) as its vertex set and is isomorphic to the edge-graph of a \(3\)-dimensional polytope, \(\mathcal{B}(V)\) is called a Reuleaux polyhedron.

The main theorem states that, given a finite subset \(V\) of at least \(4\) points of \(\mathbb{R}^3\), the following three statements are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] \(V\) has Borsuk number \(4\).
\item[(ii)] A subset of \(V\) is an extremizer for the Vázsonyi problem.
\item[(iii)] The ball polyhedron of a subset of \(V\) is a Reuleaux polyhedron.
\end{itemize}

The main ingredients of the proof are a result on the chromatic number of an involutive polyhedral graph and a proof of a conjecture of \textit{Y. Kupitz}, \textit{H. Martini} and \textit{M. Perles} [Acta Math. Hung. 126, No. 1--2, 99--163 (2010; Zbl 1224.52025)] stating that, given an extremizer \(V\) for the Vázsonyi problem, \(G(V)\) is isomorphic to the edge-graph of a \(3\)-dimensional polytope if and only if
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] no proper subset of \(V\) is an extremizer for the Vázsonyi problem and
\item[(ii)] all the points in \(V\) have unit distance with at least three distinct points from \(V\).
\end{itemize}
